distinguishing_features: Active impressed-current cathodic polarization of the duct steel to an immunity potential, instead of molybdate inhibitor dosing that raises pitting potential.
External Ti/Pt-Ir inert anodes and a DC rectifier sized to the wetted duct area, instead of a chemical day tank and peristaltic dosing pumps.
Reference-electrode feedback control of steel potential, instead of schedule-driven inhibitor addition.
Anode placement and current-density sizing for acidic condensate films and pools in an FGD duct, rather than absorber-loop alloy passivation.
parsed.objective_technical_problem: Suppress anodic dissolution of carbon-steel duct surfaces exposed to acidic, conductive sulfate/chloride condensate where coating defects or discontinuities expose metal.
parsed.viable_reason: The current-demand analysis is dimensionally wrong and understates acid-polarization current by orders of magnitude (1-5 mA/cm^2 is 10-50 A/m^2 before Tafel amplification), so the 50 A/m^2 anode sizing cannot plausibly hold the duct steel at immunity in pH 1-3 condensate.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: ICCP with inert anodes, DC rectifiers, reference electrodes, and potential feedback is a conventional corrosion-control toolkit, so substituting it for the inhibitor-dosing mechanism and applying routine sizing/control to the same corrosion problem would not be an inventive step.
